newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico seen tapping debt markets in 1997 - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Mexico seen tapping debt markets in 1997 - analyst.

text.p: Mexico's strong presence in global capital markets will extend into early 1997, even though its amortizations next year will shrink, Merrill Lynch managing director Joyce Chang said Thursday.

In a move to head off any concern about a large amount of debt coming due in 1998 and 1999, the United Mexican States is seen continuing to issue debt in its traditional markets and in wider range of European currencies, Chang said in an interview before speaking at a conference on global investment management.

Mexico will likely focus on repaying more of the $3.5 billion it still owes to the United States as part of the bailout package put together by the Clinton administration after the 1994-95 crash of the peso, she added.
"I think that Mexico will be in the markets more because their amortizations in 1998 and 1999 are still relatively heavy," she said.

"I think that the strategy of the government will be to use the fact that they had a very good year (in 1996) in the markets to raise further funds in the first half of next year, so that as 1998 approaches people in the market will not be worried that they cannot make those payments...," she said.
The United Mexico States has only about $1.4 billion in market debt coming due in 1997, but other state-run agencies will have to go to the market as well.
Mexico also has large obligations to the International Monetary Fund and other multilateral organizations coming due toward the end of the century.

Mexico is presently renegotiating a new three-year IMF loan program and is considering prepaying a further $1.0 billion, on top of the $1.0 billion it has already prepayed and $1.0 billion coming due next year.
"With the IMF now negotiating an agreement to go through the year 2000, they can essentially have that profile that humps up now spread more across that period," Chang said..
"So I think they will very clearly look more at retiring more of the U.S. Treasury debt -- the $3.5 billion -- because that is not a natural source of lending for Mexico," she said.
The federal government has recently placed its external debt in the U.S. dollars, Japanese yen and German marks.
But Chang added, "I think will continue with it and they will likely add some other currencies, like the Argentines have."
"I think that they could add sterling, shillings and French francs and others, and I think they are keenly aware that they would like to have more of a presence in the European market," she said.
However, the size of Mexican issues will likely shrink.
"I think that the period where they have these mega-issues -- that are $6.0 billion or $1.0 billion -- is over, so I would expect smaller maturities," she said.
Mexico could also selectively buy back some more of its Brady bonds, she added.
